title: Determinant Proofs — Exercise 5.2
notes: $$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ bc & ca & ab \end{vmatrix} = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ bc & ca & ab \end{vmatrix}$$
Applying column operations $C_1 \to C_1 - C_2$ and $C_2 \to C_2 - C_3$:
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ a-b & b-c & c \\ bc-ca & ca-ab & ab \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ b+c & c+a & a+b \end{vmatrix} = (b-c)(c-a)(a-b)(a+b+c)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ b+c & c+a & a+b \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ a+b+c & a+b+c & a+b+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (a+b+c) \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (a+b+c) \begin{vmatrix} a-b & b-c & c \\ a^2-b^2 & b^2-c^2 & c^2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ a^3 & b^3 & c^3 \end{vmatrix} = (b-c)(c-a)(a-b)(a+b+c)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ a^3 & b^3 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ a-b & b-c & c \\ a^3-b^3 & b^3-c^3 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
Factoring $x^3 - y^3 = (x-y)(x^2 + xy + y^2)$, take $(a-b)$ common from $C_1$ and $(b-c)$ common from $C_2$:
$$\begin{vmatrix} x & y & z \\ x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ yz & zx & xy \end{vmatrix} = (y-z)(z-x)(x-y)(yz+zx+xy)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} x & y & z \\ x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ yz & zx & xy \end{vmatrix}$$
Multiply $C_1, C_2, C_3$ by $x, y, z$ respectively and divide by $xyz$:
$$= \frac{1}{xyz} \begin{vmatrix} x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ x^3 & y^3 & z^3 \\ xyz & xyz & xyz \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \frac{xyz}{xyz} \begin{vmatrix} x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ x^3 & y^3 & z^3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ x^3 & y^3 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ x^2-y^2 & y^2-z^2 & z^2 \\ x^3-y^3 & y^3-z^3 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (x-y)(y-z) \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ x+y & y+z & z^2 \\ x^2+xy+y^2 & y^2+yz+z^2 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} b+c & a & b \\ c+a & c & a \\ a+b & b & c \end{vmatrix} = (a+b+c)(a-c)^2$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} b+c & a & b \\ c+a & c & a \\ a+b & b & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} (b+c)-a-b & a & b \\ (c+a)-c-a & c & a \\ (a+b)-b-c & b & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} c-a & a & b \\ 0 & c & a \\ -(c-a) & b & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (c-a) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & b \\ 0 & c & a \\ -1 & b & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (c-a) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & b \\ 0 & c & a \\ 0 & a+b & b+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} 1+a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ a_1 & 1+a_2 & a_3 \\ a_1 & a_2 & 1+a_3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} a^2 & bc & c^2+ac \\ a^2+ab & b^2 & ac \\ ab & b^2+bc & c^2 \end{vmatrix} = 4a^2b^2c^2$$
Observe that each column can be written as a scalar multiple of a simpler column:
$$C_1 = a\begin{pmatrix} a \\ a+b \\ b \end{pmatrix}, \quad C_2 = b\begin{pmatrix} c \\ b \\ b+c \end{pmatrix}, \quad C_3 = c\begin{pmatrix} c+a \\ a \\ c \end{pmatrix}$$
Taking $a, b, c$ common from $C_1, C_2, C_3$ respectively:
$$\text{LHS} = abc \begin{vmatrix} a & c & c+a \\ a+b & b & a \\ b & b+c & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= abc \begin{vmatrix} 2(a+b) & 2(b+c) & 2(c+a) \\ a+b & b & a \\ b & b+c & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 2abc \begin{vmatrix} a+b & b+c & c+a \\ a+b & b & a \\ b & b+c & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 2abc \begin{vmatrix} 0 & c & c \\ a+b & b & a \\ b & b+c & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 2abc \cdot c \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ a+b & b & a \\ b & b+c & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} x^2+1 & xy & xz \\ xy & y^2+1 & yz \\ xz & yz & z^2+1 \end{vmatrix} = 1+x^2+y^2+z^2$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} x^2+1 & xy & xz \\ xy & y^2+1 & yz \\ xz & yz & z^2+1 \end{vmatrix}$$
Multiply $R_1, R_2, R_3$ by $x, y, z$ respectively and divide by $xyz$ (as in Q(iv)):
$$= \frac{1}{xyz}\begin{vmatrix} x^3+x & x^2y & x^2z \\ xy^2 & y^3+y & y^2z \\ xz^2 & yz^2 & z^3+z \end{vmatrix}$$
Taking $x$ common from $C_1$, $y$ common from $C_2$, $z$ common from $C_3$:

$$= \frac{xyz}{xyz}\begin{vmatrix} x^2+1 & x^2 & x^2 \\ y^2 & y^2+1 & y^2 \\ z^2 & z^2 & z^2+1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} x^2+1 & x^2 & x^2 \\ y^2 & y^2+1 & y^2 \\ z^2 & z^2 & z^2+1 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} b+c & a & a \\ b & c+a & b \\ c & c & a+b \end{vmatrix} = 4abc$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} b+c & a & a \\ b & c+a & b \\ c & c & a+b \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 2(b+c) & 2(a+c) & 2(a+b) \\ b & c+a & b \\ c & c & a+b \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 2\begin{vmatrix} b+c & a+c & a+b \\ b & c+a & b \\ c & c & a+b \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 2\begin{vmatrix} b & a & 0 \\ b & c+a & b \\ c & c & a+b \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 2\begin{vmatrix} b & a & 0 \\ 0 & c & b \\ c & c & a+b \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} a+b & b+c & c+a \\ b+c & c+a & a+b \\ c+a & a+b & b+c \end{vmatrix} = 2(3abc-a^3-b^3-c^3)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} a+b & b+c & c+a \\ b+c & c+a & a+b \\ c+a & a+b & b+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 2(a+b+c) & 2(a+b+c) & 2(a+b+c) \\ b+c & c+a & a+b \\ c+a & a+b & b+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 2(a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ b+c & c+a & a+b \\ c+a & a+b & b+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= 2(a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ b+c & a-b & a-c \\ c+a & b-c & b-a \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2-bc \\ 1 & b & b^2-ca \\ 1 & c & c^2-ab \end{vmatrix} = 0$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2-bc \\ 1 & b & b^2-ca \\ 1 & c & c^2-ab \end{vmatrix}$$
Since $R_2$ and $R_3$ are identical, the determinant is zero:
$$\begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & 1+x^3 \\ y & y^2 & 1+y^3 \\ z & z^2 & 1+z^3 \end{vmatrix} = 0$$
Splitting $C_3$ using linearity of determinants ($C_3 = C_3' + C_3''$ where $C_3'=(1,1,1)^T$ and $C_3''=(x^3,y^3,z^3)^T$):
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & 1 \\ y & y^2 & 1 \\ z & z^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & x^3 \\ y & y^2 & y^3 \\ z & z^2 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
Taking $x, y, z$ common from $R_1, R_2, R_3$ of the second determinant:
$$= \begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & 1 \\ y & y^2 & 1 \\ z & z^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + xyz\begin{vmatrix} 1 & x & x^2 \\ 1 & y & y^2 \\ 1 & z & z^2 \end{vmatrix}$$
A cyclic rearrangement of columns (an even permutation) shows the first determinant equals the second (Vandermonde) determinant, call it $D$:
$$\begin{vmatrix} b^2+c^2 & a^2 & a^2 \\ b^2 & c^2+a^2 & b^2 \\ c^2 & c^2 & a^2+b^2 \end{vmatrix} = 4a^2b^2c^2$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} B+C & A & A \\ B & C+A & B \\ C & C & A+B \end{vmatrix}$$
This is exactly the same form proved in Q(xi), which equals $4ABC$. Substituting back $A=a^2, B=b^2, C=c^2$:
$$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix} = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 0 & b-a & b^2-a^2 \\ 0 & c-a & c^2-a^2 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & 1+px^3 \\ y & y^2 & 1+py^3 \\ z & z^2 & 1+pz^3 \end{vmatrix} = (1+pxyz)(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & 1 \\ y & y^2 & 1 \\ z & z^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + p\begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & x^3 \\ y & y^2 & y^3 \\ z & z^2 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
Taking $x, y, z$ common from the rows of the second determinant, and using the Vandermonde result of Q(xvi), $D=(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)$:
Note: putting $p=1$ and using $xyz+1=0$ reduces this directly to the result of Q(xiv).
$$\begin{vmatrix} x+a & b & c \\ a & x+b & c \\ a & b & x+c \end{vmatrix} = x^2(x+a+b+c)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} x+a & b & c \\ a & x+b & c \\ a & b & x+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} x+a+b+c & b & c \\ x+a+b+c & x+b & c \\ x+a+b+c & b & x+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (x+a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & b & c \\ 1 & x+b & c \\ 1 & b & x+c \end{vmatrix}$$
